title: The Native Speaker Myth

pts: Native-speakerism is the largely unexamined belief that native English speakers are inherently better, more authoritative English teachers than proficient non-native speakers.
This assumption persists in hiring practices, learner preferences, and institutional marketing across much of the global ELT industry.
Naming it explicitly, as this poster does, is the first step toward genuinely examining its actual validity.

v: Eight short statements on slips (see model language); chart paper

items: Give each group eight statements about English teachers, collected from everyday talk (see model language).
Groups sort them into three piles: ‘evidence-based’, ‘assumption’ and ‘not sure’.
For each ‘assumption’, groups write the hidden belief underneath it.
Introduce Holliday’s term native-speakerism and check whether the hidden beliefs fit it.
In a DIET pre-service course, trainees collect such statements during school visits.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Statements for sorting (written for this book):

lines: ‘Our school has a native speaker, so our spoken English is better.’
‘She’s good, but she’s not a native speaker.’
‘Learners need to hear real English.’
‘I don’t teach pronunciation because my own accent is Indian.’
A: ‘Real English’. That assumes English from India isn’t real.
B: And ‘but she’s not a native speaker’ treats it as a weakness even when she’s good.
A: So the hidden belief is: there is one true owner of English, and it isn’t us.

blocks.x: Naming a belief does not settle whether it is true, but it makes examination possible.

body: Purpose: to show native-speakerism as a hidden assumption beneath everyday remarks. Content: an iceberg; above the waterline, speech bubbles such as ‘real English’ and ‘native accent preferred’; below it, the label ‘belief: native speakers are the best teachers’. Style: clean diagram, labels in plain type. Board version: a triangle with a wavy line across it and words above and below.

items: Mentimeter (free plan, limited questions) for anonymous collection of statements.

blocks.x: Slips of paper sorted into three piles on the desk.

points.sub: A less clear category than assumed
pts: The 'native speaker' category itself is linguistically less clear-cut than commonly assumed, given the genuine plurality established in Unit 78's World Englishes work.
Which variety counts as sufficiently 'native' often reflects prestige and politics as much as any linguistic criterion.
This conceptual instability undermines native-speaker status as a straightforward, objective hiring or quality criterion.

items: Distribute six speaker profiles (see model language).
Individually, participants decide whether each person is a ‘native speaker of English’.
Groups compare and list the criteria they used: age of acquisition, country, accent, dominance, identity, proficiency.
Introduce Rampton’s (1990) distinction between expertise, affiliation and inheritance.
Discuss which of these three matters for teaching.
Participants write their own language profile and apply the same criteria to themselves.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Ananya, born in Bengaluru, English-medium from nursery, uses English at home with her parents alongside Kannada.
Tomás, born in Manchester to Chilean parents, speaks English all day and Spanish at weekends.
Joseph, a Nigerian journalist, has used English since primary school and writes in it daily.
T: Who is a native speaker?
S1: Tomás, definitely.
S2: Why not Ananya? She learned English at the same age.
S3: Maybe because of the accent. Or because she’s Indian.

blocks.x: The criterion that decides the answer is often place of birth or appearance, not language (Davies 2003).

body: Purpose: to show that ‘native speaker’ is a continuum shaped by several criteria. Content: six figures arranged along a curved band shading from dark to light, with labels for age of acquisition, use, identity and recognition by others; there is no sharp line. Style: calm infographic. Board version: a line with six dots and a question mark in the middle.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for printable profile cards.

pts: Being a native speaker demonstrates proficiency in the language, not competence in teaching it — these are genuinely distinct skill sets.
Proficient non-native-speaking teachers often have superior metalinguistic awareness, having consciously learned the grammatical system themselves.
This directly echoes Unit 6's point about explicit grammar knowledge — something many native speakers themselves lack for their own language.

v: Five learner questions about grammar on cards

items: Present five questions that learners commonly ask (see model language).
Participants write a short, accurate explanation that a Class 8 learner could follow.
Compare answers in groups and choose the clearest.
Discuss: would a proficient but untrained speaker be able to give these explanations? What knowledge did you draw on?
Link to Unit 6: explicit knowledge about grammar is learned, not inherited.
Replace grammar questions with pronunciation questions (for example, why -ed sounds different in walked, played and wanted).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Why do we say ‘I have lived here since 2019’ but not ‘I have lived here in 2019’?
Why can’t I say ‘I am knowing the answer’?

blocks.x: One trainee’s explanation of the third:

lines: Some verbs describe states, not actions: know, like, own, believe. We don’t usually use them in the -ing form, because -ing shows something in progress.

blocks.x: Proficiency produces I know the answer; teaching expertise explains the choice, anticipates the error and plans practice. Medgyes (1994) noted that non-native teachers often have stronger explicit knowledge because they had to learn the system consciously.

body: Purpose: to separate language proficiency from teaching expertise. Content: two overlapping circles, one labelled ‘using English’ (fluency, range, accuracy) and one labelled ‘teaching English’ (explanation, planning, feedback, knowledge of learners), with a small overlap. Style: simple Venn diagram. Board version: two circles and a few words in each.

items: Google Docs (free) for pooling explanations across groups.

blocks.x: Answers written on chart paper and displayed as a gallery.

pts: Non-native-speaking teachers can model the L2 learning process itself, offering genuinely relatable, empathetic guidance native speakers cannot.
They often have direct, personal insight into their own learners' specific L1-related challenges (Unit 49's transfer errors).
These are genuine pedagogical advantages, not merely compensations for lacking native proficiency.
points.who: George Braine's research on non-native English-speaking teachers

items: Participants recall one difficulty they had when learning English, and how they overcame it.
In pairs, they turn that experience into a classroom tip for today’s learners.
Groups list difficulties that come from specific home languages (for example, article use for speakers of Kannada, Hindi or Tamil, which have no articles), linking to Unit 49.
Discuss Medgyes’s list of non-native teacher advantages and add examples from the group.
Each participant writes one sentence beginning ‘Because I learned English myself, I can…’.
Invite a senior teacher to tell the story of learning English through a Kannada- or Urdu-medium school, and ask trainees to note the strategies she mentions.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Sentences from a DIET workshop (written for this book):

lines: Because I learned English myself, I can tell learners that mistakes with ‘the’ are normal and show them the pattern that helped me.
Because I speak Telugu, I can predict why learners say ‘He is having two brothers’ and explain it in a way they recognize.

blocks.x: Braine (1999) and Medgyes (1994) present these as genuine pedagogical strengths, not consolations for lacking native status.

body: Purpose: to show the non-native teacher as a guide who has made the same journey. Content: a winding hill path; a teacher partway up turns to help a group of learners, with small signposts marked ‘articles’, ‘listening’ and ‘confidence’. Style: warm illustration, Indian landscape. Board version: a zigzag line with a stick figure and a few labelled flags.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) to collect ‘Because I learned English myself…’ sentences.

blocks.x: Sentences written on strips and pinned to a staff-room board.

pts: Job advertisements and hiring practices in many contexts still explicitly or implicitly favour native-speaker candidates, regardless of actual qualification.
This constitutes genuine, documented discrimination against equally or more qualified non-native-speaking teachers.
This connects directly to Unit 59's discussion of native-speakerism — this is a genuine, concrete professional-ethics issue facing the field.

v: Six job advertisements (real, anonymized, or written for the session)

items: Give groups six advertisements for English teaching posts.
Groups highlight every requirement and label it: qualification, experience, teaching skill, proficiency, or identity (nationality, ‘native speaker’, accent, appearance).
Groups decide which requirements are defensible as indicators of teaching quality.
Rewrite one advertisement so that every criterion can be demonstrated by any qualified applicant.
Discuss the evidence on hiring discrimination (Clark and Paran 2007) and TESOL’s position statement.
Survey advertisements in a local newspaper or on a recruitment site over one month and report the pattern.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Wanted: Native English speaker for spoken English classes. Neutral accent. Passport holders from UK/USA/Canada/Australia preferred.

Wanted: English teacher for spoken English classes. Required: a recognized teaching qualification, proficiency at C1 or above, and evidence of effective speaking lessons (a demonstration class will form part of selection).

blocks.x: Clark and Paran’s (2007) survey of UK language schools found that many employers regarded native-speaker status as important in recruitment, which disadvantaged qualified non-native applicants. Unit 59 raised this as critical awareness; here it is professional ethics.

body: Figure 96.5 What the advertisement really asks for

Purpose: to expose non-pedagogical criteria in job advertisements. Content: an advertisement on a noticeboard with some phrases circled in red (‘native speaker’, ‘passport holders’) and others ticked in green (‘qualification’, ‘demonstration class’). Style: realistic but simple. Board version: a rectangle with words underlined in two ways.

items: TEFL Equity Advocates (free website run by Marek Kiczkowiak) for articles and resources on fair hiring [VERIFY current availability].

blocks.x: Photocopied or handwritten advertisements and two colours of pen.

pts: Some learners genuinely express a preference for native-speaking teachers, reflecting internalised native-speakerism rather than evidence-based judgement.
This connects to Unit 78's variety-preference discussion — this preference is real and worth understanding, without simply validating its premise.
Institutions can educate learners about this issue, rather than simply catering to an unexamined preference.

v: A short survey; a discussion task card

items: Learners complete an anonymous survey: ‘What makes a good English teacher?’ and ‘Would you prefer a native-speaking teacher? Why?’
Share the class results without comment.
In groups, learners sort the reasons they gave into ‘about language skill’, ‘about teaching skill’ and ‘about image or status’.
Groups discuss which reasons are about the teacher and which are about assumptions.
For adults or parents, run the survey at a school open day and discuss the results in a parents’ meeting.
Support: provide sentence starters (A good teacher explains… / A good teacher understands…).
Challenge: learners summarize one research finding on learner preferences.

blocks.x: A class discussion (written for this book):

lines: S1: A native speaker has a perfect accent.
T: Which accent do you want to understand best?
S2: Actually, the people I will talk to are in Chennai, Dubai and Singapore.
S3: My best teacher explained in Tamil when we got lost. A foreign teacher couldn’t do that.
T: So what are we really looking for?
Ss: Someone who teaches well and understands us.

blocks.x: The aim is not to argue learners out of their preference, but to help them examine where it came from (Unit 78).

body: Figure 96.6 Where does the preference come from?

Purpose: to trace learner preferences back to their sources. Content: a learner thinking ‘native teacher’, with streams feeding the thought: advertising, films, family advice and, smallest, ‘my own experience’. Style: friendly infographic. Board version: a head outline with four arrows pointing in.

items: Google Forms (free) for the anonymous survey and automatic charts.

blocks.x: Paper slips and a show-of-hands tally on the board.

pts: Hiring based on demonstrated teaching qualification and skill, not native-speaker status, directly addresses this documented discrimination.
Explicitly valuing and marketing non-native-speaking teachers' genuine strengths counters the myth's institutional reinforcement.
This connects to Unit 59's critical-awareness content — institutional hiring policy is itself a concrete, actionable lever here.

v: School leaders, DIET faculty, teacher educators
A current recruitment or staffing document

items: Review the institution’s current recruitment and promotion criteria for English teachers.
Mark each criterion as skill-based or status-based.
Draft replacement criteria: qualifications, demonstrated teaching, proficiency evidence, and knowledge of learners’ languages.
Design a short demonstration-lesson rubric using the approach of Unit 46.
Draft two brochure lines that present the institution’s multilingual teachers accurately.
For a government system, apply the same analysis to criteria for selecting resource persons and master trainers.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Draft policy statement (written for this book):

lines: Teachers are selected on the basis of qualification, demonstrated classroom skill and proficiency in English at the level required for the post. Knowledge of learners’ home languages is valued as a professional asset. Nationality and ‘native-speaker’ status are not selection criteria.
Our teachers have learned English as you are learning it, and they know how to help you. They use English, Kannada and Hindi to help you learn.

blocks.x: Institutional policy is one of the most direct levers against native-speakerism because it shapes who gets hired and how teachers are presented (Holliday 2005).

body: Purpose: to show a shift in recruitment criteria. Content: a pair of scales; on the left pan, a passport and a flag; on the right pan, a certificate, a lesson plan and a speech bubble with several scripts; the right side is heavier. Style: clean, symbolic. Board version: a simple balance with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) with suggestion mode, so colleagues can comment on draft criteria.

blocks.x: Printed draft circulated at a staff meeting with space for handwritten comments.

body: When presenting teachers to parents, avoid praising anyone’s ‘native-like accent’. Praise clarity, skill and results. The words an institution uses in public shape what learners and families come to value.

points.sub: What every practitioner can carry forward
pts: Evaluate teaching quality based on demonstrated skill and genuine pedagogical knowledge, not native-speaker status, in yourself and colleagues alike.
This connects directly back to this series' entire content — everything covered here is learnable, teachable expertise, independent of native-speaker status.
This is one of the clearest, most actionable applications of this tier's critical-awareness thread.

v: 30 minutes, plus a follow-up after one month

items: List five things that make you an effective English teacher, with an example of each from the past month.
Beside each, note whether it depends on where you were born, or on knowledge and skill you developed.
Write a short paragraph beginning ‘I judge teaching quality by…’.
Share with a colleague and agree to use the same criteria when observing each other (Unit 68); revisit the paragraph after a month.
Trainees include the paragraph in their teaching portfolio or practicum file.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One teacher’s stance (written for this book):

lines: I judge teaching quality by how clearly a teacher explains, how well she listens to learners, how she uses feedback and how much learners can do by the end of the term. None of these depends on a passport. Almost everything in this book, from lesson staging to rubric design, is learnable expertise.

body: Purpose: to close the unit with a positive, skill-based view of teacher quality. Content: a bookshelf of four volumes labelled Foundations, Skill Integration, Advanced Pedagogy and Theory & Research, with a teacher reaching for them; a small caption reads ‘expertise is built, not inherited’. Style: warm and dignified. Board version: four rectangles in a row with the four labels.

items: Microsoft OneNote (free) or a notes app for a digital reflective journal.

blocks.x: A page in the teaching journal, revisited after one month.

body: Next time you hear a colleague say ‘my English is not good enough’ or ‘we need a native speaker’, ask one question: ‘Good enough for what?’ Then list together the specific classroom skills that the situation actually needs.

dek: Unit 96 of 100: deconstructing native-speakerism — the widespread, largely unexamined assumption that native speakers are automatically the best English teachers.

aims.x: This unit examines one of the most persistent assumptions in English language teaching: that the best teacher of English is, by default, a native speaker of it. It shapes job advertisements, parents’ choices and many teachers’ confidence in themselves. The unit names the assumption, tests it against what we know about language and about teaching, and turns the results into practical steps for teachers, teacher educators and institutions.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define native-speakerism and recognize it in hiring, marketing and everyday talk about teachers;
explain why the category ‘native speaker’ is less clear-cut than it appears;
distinguish proficiency in English from expertise in teaching it;
identify the particular strengths that proficient non-native-speaking teachers bring to a class;
analyse job advertisements and institutional policies for discriminatory criteria;
respond thoughtfully to learners and parents who prefer native-speaking teachers;
propose fair, skill-based criteria for recruiting and evaluating English teachers;
articulate your own professional stance on teacher quality.

why: Why this matters. This assumption shapes hiring, learner preference, and institutional prestige worldwide, often with little relationship to actual teaching quality or expertise.

background.x: The idea that native speakers make ideal language teachers has a long history, but it was only named and examined systematically in the late twentieth century. Robert Phillipson (1992) called it the native speaker fallacy and traced it to the Commonwealth Conference on the Teaching of English as a Second Language held at Makerere in 1961. Adrian Holliday (2005, 2006) later coined the term native-speakerism for ‘an established belief that “native-speaker” teachers represent a “Western culture” from which spring the ideals both of the English language and of English language teaching methodology’ (Holliday 2006: 385) [VERIFY exact wording of quotation]. The belief is ideological: it survives not because evidence supports it but because it is rarely questioned.

The category itself has been challenged for decades. Ben Rampton’s (1990) proposal to replace ‘native speaker’ with the separate notions of expertise, affiliation and inheritance showed how much the label bundles together. Alan Davies (2003) concluded that the native speaker is both a myth and a reality: a real category in terms of early acquisition, but a poor guide to what a person can actually do with a language. As Unit 78 showed, a Nigerian or Indian speaker who has used English since early childhood may be as ‘native’ in any linguistic sense as a speaker from Leeds, yet is rarely treated as one in the job market.

Research on non-native-speaking teachers began to grow in the 1990s. Péter Medgyes (1994) argued that the two groups are different rather than better or worse, and listed the advantages of non-native teachers: they model a successful learner, teach learning strategies, supply information about the language, anticipate difficulties, show empathy, and can use the learners’ own language. George Braine’s edited collection (1999) gave non-native teacher educators a collective voice, and TESOL International Association issued a formal position statement against discrimination in hiring (TESOL 2006) [VERIFY year and title of the position statement].

For India the question is not abstract. Almost all English teachers in Indian schools are multilingual Indians. Yet ‘native accent’ and ‘foreign faculty’ still appear in advertisements for coaching centres and private schools, and many teachers speak apologetically about ‘our English’. NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 both place the learner’s home languages and the multilingual teacher at the centre of language education (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). This unit argues that the multilingual Indian teacher of English is not a substitute for a missing ideal, but a professional with distinctive expertise.

items: Discourse analysis. A short analysis of ten statements or advertisements, identifying native-speakerist assumptions and explaining each.
Revised advertisement or policy. A rewritten job advertisement or recruitment policy with skill-based criteria and a rationale.
Learner discussion plan. A lesson plan that helps learners examine their preferences, with the survey, the task and expected outcomes.
Stance statement. A reflective paragraph on teacher quality, with evidence from one month of practice.
When have you spoken apologetically about your own English? What prompted it?
Which of your strengths as a teacher come from having learned English yourself?
How does your school present its English teachers to parents?
If you sat on a selection panel tomorrow, what would you ask candidates to demonstrate?
How would you respond to a parent who asks for a ‘native-speaker’ teacher?

terms.def: Three separate ways of relating to a language: how well a person uses it, how far they identify with it, and whether they were born into it (Rampton 1990). The distinction challenges the idea of the ‘native speaker’.

What learners say they want from teaching, for example a particular accent model or type of teacher; preferences are worth researching and discussing, but they are often shaped by assumptions rather than by learners’ real communicative needs.

Unfair treatment of people on the basis of their language, dialect or accent, for example rejecting a qualified teacher because of a regional Indian accent rather than for any problem with intelligibility.

The ability to reflect on language as an object, noticing and talking about its forms and rules; multilingual learners often show this ability strongly, comparing structures across Kannada, Hindi and English.
The mistaken belief that the ideal teacher of English is a native speaker (Phillipson 1992); expertise, training and multilingual awareness matter more than a teacher’s first language.
An ideology that treats ‘native speakers’ and their cultures as the model for English and its teaching, and so disadvantages other teachers and varieties (Holliday 2006).
A teacher whose first language is not English; most English teachers in the world are in this position, and many bring valuable multilingual awareness and shared learning experience to the classroom.

Hiring English teachers on the basis of qualifications, language proficiency and teaching skill rather than native-speaker status. It is presented as a fairer, more ethical alternative to native-speakerism in recruitment.

How teachers see themselves as professionals, shaped by their histories, language backgrounds, communities and work. For non-native-speaking teachers of English in India, a confident identity is an important professional resource.
